description: Question: does a bigger genome mean more genes? If DNA were mostly genes, gene count would grow in proportion to genome size (genes ∝ size^b with b = 1). Data: 1,000 annotated reference genomes from NCBI Datasets, the first 200 of each of five groups (bacteria, archaea, fungi, plants, animals): assembly size, G+C % and protein-coding gene count. Steps: per genome the size in Mb and the gene density (genes per Mb); per group a least-squares fit of log10(genes) on log10(size), whose slope b is the scaling exponent, with R², and the fold ranges of size and gene count; the same for prokaryotes against eukaryotes. Aha: in bacteria b = 1.01 (R² 0.99) and archaea 0.88: a prokaryote genome is genes packed end to end, about 900–1,000 per Mb at any size. In eukaryotes the law breaks: animal genomes span a 500-fold range of size (57 Mb to the axolotl's 29 Gb) with b = 0.15, plants 0.26, fungi 0.53, and the median density falls to 25 genes per Mb in animals. Genome size says little about gene number or complexity: the C-value paradox. The extra DNA is introns, repeats and transposable elements, which this data does not hold. Caveats: NCBI's first 200 reference genomes per group are a sample in NCBI's order, not random, and over-represent well-studied species; gene counts depend on the annotation pipeline (RefSeq or submitter), and polyploids (wheat, 104k genes) count every copy; assembly length is not flow-cytometry C-value (repeats may be missing from assemblies); microsporidia (Encephalitozoon) count as fungi. Next: hover a genome; drill down to one group (insects, grasses: any NCBI taxon id in the same query); expand to repeat content or intron length, or to Lynch's population-size hypothesis.
name: The C-value paradox: genome size against gene number
